questions.question: Does the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantee a real root for every polynomial?
options: Yes, because nonreal roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs.
Yes, but only for polynomials of even degree.
No; the roots are guaranteed in $\mathbb{C}$, not necessarily in $\mathbb{R}$.
No; it guarantees a root only when the coefficients are real.

questions.question: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra say about the field $\mathbb{C}$ from the viewpoint of polynomial equations?
options: Only polynomials with real coefficients are guaranteed a complex root.
Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.
Every complex polynomial, constants included, has a complex root.
Every nonconstant complex polynomial has $n$ distinct complex roots.

questions.question: How many complex roots does a degree-$3$ polynomial have when counted with multiplicity?
options: It depends on whether the roots are real.

questions.question: Is $p(z)=7$ covered by the root guarantee in the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra?
options: Yes, because $7$ is complex.
Yes, because every polynomial has degree at least $1$.
No, because it is a constant polynomial.
No, because it has real coefficients.

questions.question: What is the root of $p(z)=z^3$ and what is its multiplicity?
options: $3$ with multiplicity $1$
$0$ with multiplicity $3$
$1$ with multiplicity $3$
$0$ with multiplicity $1$ only

questions.question: Why does linear factorisation follow from the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra?
options: Each real root yields a linear factor; nonreal roots stay quadratic.
The theorem gives all $n$ roots at once, with no division needed.
Each root divides the constant term, which gives a linear factor.
Each complex root yields a linear factor; repeat by degree.

questions.question: Why is the zero polynomial not a good test case for the “exactly $n$ roots” statement?
options: It has no roots, like every nonzero constant polynomial
Every complex number is a root, with no well-defined degree
Its only root is $0$, so it would have exactly one root
It has finitely many roots, but none with a defined multiplicity

questions.question: For $p(z)=(z^2+1)^2$, why do both roots have multiplicity $2$?
options: Because every non-real root automatically has multiplicity $2$.
Because $p(z)=(z-\mathrm{i})^2(z+\mathrm{i})^2$.
Because the polynomial has degree $4$, so each root must appear four times.
Because $z^2+1$ has no complex roots before squaring.

questions.question: Consider the polynomial $p(z)=z^5-1$ with $z\in\mathbb{C}$. Which statement correctly describes its roots?
options: It has one root in $\mathbb{R}$ and five more in $\mathbb{C}$, six in total.
It has five roots in $\mathbb{C}$, and exactly one of them, $z=1$, is real.
It has only the root $z=1$, since $1$ has a single fifth root.
It has five roots in $\mathbb{C}$, and two of them, $z=\pm1$, are real.
